title: Focused transthoracic echocardiography in acute pulmonary embolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy.
abstract: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography is the diagnostic gold standard for acute pulmonary embolism, but delays and radiation risks necessitate rapid bedside alternatives. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of isolated point-of-care focused echocardiography and a combined approach of focused echocardiography and lower limb deep vein ultrasound for suspected acute pulmonary embolism. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Adult patients presenting to acute healthcare settings with suspected acute pulmonary embolism. Specific morphological signs [dilated right ventricle (RV), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion] and highly specific functional signs [McConnell's sign, the 60/60 sign, abnormal interventricular motion, RV outflow tract early systolic notching (ESN), and clot-in-transit] assessed via isolated focused echocardiography, alongside a combined echocardiography and deep vein ultrasound strategy. Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis to determine pooled sensitivity and specificity. Thirty-three studies (3981 patients) were included. Isolated focused echocardiography signs demonstrated poor sensitivities (0.03-0.65) but high specificities, including McConnell's sign (0.98), the 60/60 sign (0.93), and RV outflow tract ESN (0.98). The combined echocardiography and deep vein ultrasound approach yielded a pooled sensitivity of 0.62 and a pooled specificity of 0.98. In this meta-analysis, isolated focused echocardiography signs demonstrated a reportedly low sensitivity but high specificity for the diagnosis of acute pulmonary embolism. Integrating lower limb deep vein ultrasound improves diagnostic sensitivity, though definitive exclusion still requires computed tomography.

title: Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography-based radiomics for predicting risk groups, tumor stage, and capsular and fat tissue invasion in thymomas.
abstract: Purpose This study aimed to investigate the predictive value of fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography (CT) based radiomics in patients with thymoma for risk stratification and tumor staging, including capsular and fat tissue invasion. Methods A total of 67 (50 for training and 17 for validation) patients with thymoma were analyzed. Thymomas were categorized as low risk (types A, AB, and B1) or high risk (types B2 and B3) and as early stage (I-II) or advanced stage (III-IV). PET- and CT-derived radiomic features extracted. Three models were constructed: a PET model, a CT model, and a PET/CT (combined) model. Feature selection was conducted using the Mann-Whitney U test and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression. Results For risk group discrimination, the combined model demonstrated the highest performance [area under the curve (AUC) = 0.80], outperforming the PET (AUC = 0.78) and CT (AUC = 0.72) models. In stage discrimination, the PET model and the combined model achieved superior performance (AUC = 0.82 for both), compared with the CT-based model (AUC = 0.75). For capsular invasion detection, predictive performance was achieved only with CT-based radiomics (AUC = 0.70). For fat tissue invasion detection, the combined model achieved the highest performance (AUC = 0.79), followed by CT (AUC = 0.76) and PET (AUC = 0.70). Maximum standardized uptake value of thymomas showed no significant discriminative value across any clinical categories ( P > 0.05). Conclusion F luorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT-based radiomics may provide complementary, noninvasive biomarkers for the management of patients with thymoma.

title: The utility of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography in relapsing polychondritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Relapsing polychondritis is a rare chronic autoimmune inflammation of the cartilage associated with life-threatening respiratory complications. Currently, no clear role of imaging modalities such as 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/computed tomography (CT) is defined in the literature. This systematic review and meta-analysis provide current evidence on the PET-positivity rate and utility in relapsing polychondritis. Prospective or retrospective studies with more than five patients of suspected relapsing polychondritis who underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT during their management and reported a PET-positivity rate were included. Low-sample-size studies describing chondritis due to other aetiologies or utilizing PET-based radiopharmaceuticals other than FDG were excluded. A systematic search using relevant keywords was conducted across four databases (PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science) to include studies up to 25 April 2025. The Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools were used for risk-of-bias analysis. Data were analysed using the R software package (v4.3.1; 2023). Out of 962 articles, three with a total of 97 patients were included. With a pooled PET-positivity rate of 94% [95% confidence interval (CI): 73-99%, I2 = 0%, P = 0.76] and a pooled baseline SUVmax of 4.0 (95% CI: 3.5-4.6, I2 = 32%, P = 0.23), 18F-FDG PET identified asymptomatic cartilage involvement in more than 25% patients and PET parameters correlated well with inflammatory markers. It had a higher positivity rate for inaccessible sites, such as peripheral airways, and was crucial in treatment monitoring. The pooled PET-positivity rate of 18F-FDG PET in relapsing polychondritis is high but requires prospective large-sample-size studies to explore the diagnostic accuracy and prognostic implications of 18F-FDG PET in relapsing polychondritis.

title: PET-derived metabolic-immunonutritional SUVmax-lactate dehydrogenase-albumin-lymphocyte index for survival prediction in human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-positive metastatic breast cancer receiving pertuzumab-based therapy.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the prognostic value of the PET-derived SUVmax-lactate dehydrogenase-albumin-lymphocyte (SUV-LAL) index in human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive metastatic breast cancer treated with pertuzumab. Methods This retrospective single-center study included patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer treated with pertuzumab-containing regimens between January 2018 and October 2025. Baseline clinical, pathological, laboratory, and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography data were retrospectively collected. The SUV-LAL index was calculated as (primary tumor maximum standardized uptake value × lactate dehydrogenase)/(albumin × absolute lymphocyte count). Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression analyses. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and time-dependent ROC analyses were performed to assess prognostic performance. Results A total of 80 patients were included, of whom 36 (45.0%) died during follow-up. The SUV-LAL index remained an independent prognostic factor for OS in multivariate analysis [hazard ratio = 1.755, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.053-2.927; P = 0.031], together with the number of pertuzumab cycles (hazard ratio = 0.921, 95% CI = 0.872-0.972; P = 0.003). Patients with a high SUV-LAL index had significantly shorter OS and PFS than those with a low SUV-LAL index (log-rank P < 0.001 and P = 0.002, respectively). ROC analysis yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.760. Compared with its individual components, the SUV-LAL index showed the strongest association with OS in univariate Cox regression analysis and achieved the highest 1-year time-dependent AUC (0.735), while maintaining acceptable prognostic performance at 3 years (AUC = 0.705). Conclusion The PET-derived SUV-LAL index independently predicts OS in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer treated with pertuzumab.

title: Predictive value of metabolic and tumor dissemination parameters in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: can relapse be predicted despite adequate interim PET response?
abstract: Objective To evaluate associations of baseline and interim fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography parameters with early clinical outcomes in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and identify prognostic/predictive biomarkers, including predictors of discordance between interim PET (iPET) response and clinical outcome. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 112 patients with DLBCL. Baseline clinical/biochemical data and metabolic parameters from staging PET (sPET) and iPET were recorded, and delta (Δ) parameters were calculated. iPET response was classified by Deauville criteria, while follow-up outcomes were categorized as remission or refractory/progressive disease. Group comparisons and receiver operating characteristic analyses were performed. Results iPET predicted outcomes with 79% sensitivity, 71% specificity, 74% accuracy, 82% negative predictive value, and 66% positive predictive value. Baseline dissemination metrics, including maximum distance between the two most distant lesions and maximum distance between the outermost voxels of the two most distant lesions PET (DmaxVoxPET), were higher in patients developing relapse/progression despite adequate iPET response [area under the curve (AUC): 0.81 and 0.77]; iPET-derived metabolic parameters - maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax), mean standardized uptake value (SUVmean), peak standardized uptake value (SUVpeak), lesion-to-liver ratio (RLL), total lesion glycolysis, and ΔSUVmax, ΔSUVmean, ΔSUVpeak, and ΔRLL significantly predicted remission (AUC: 0.70-0.79), generally outperforming baseline parameters. SUV-based indices and RLL outperformed TLG, while SUV metrics performed comparably. Ferritin was the only predictive clinical/biochemical variable (AUC: 0.79). According to multivariate logistic regression analysis, advanced-stage disease (P = 0.002) and elevated ferritin levels (P = 0.009) were found to be independent risk factors for disease progression. Conclusion iPET provides robust early response assessment and stronger predictive value than sPET in DLBCL, particularly through SUV-based parameters and RLL. While sPET reflects tumor burden and dissemination, baseline dissemination metrics may identify patients at risk of relapse despite favorable iPET findings, supporting risk-adapted management and closer surveillance.

title: Comprehensive acceptance testing and quality control of Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography/Computed Tomography systems.
abstract: Background Single photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT) systems play a crucial role in nuclear medicine for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning. Ensuring high image quality through rigorous acceptance testing and quality control is essential to maintain diagnostic reliability and patient safety. Objective This study evaluated the performance of SPECT/CT systems at NORI Hospital Islamabad against National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) and International Atomic Energy Agency standards and developed a structured quality control program based on acceptance testing results. Methods Acceptance tests were carried out using Tc-99m, I-131, and Co-57 radioactive sources, in conjunction with quadrant bar and Jaszczak phantoms. Parameters assessed included spatial resolution, intrinsic and extrinsic uniformity, energy resolution, sensitivity, center of rotation (COR), detector shielding, background counts, leakage, CT number accuracy, and nuclear medicine/CT registration. Data were compared with manufacturer specifications and NEMA standards to evaluate system performance and inform quality control strategies. Results Both detectors exhibited intrinsic and extrinsic uniformity within NEMA limits, ensuring consistent image quality. Spatial resolution testing confirmed sharp and precise imaging, while energy resolution was within manufacturer-specified values. Sensitivity measurements showed minor differences between detectors but remained within acceptable ranges. COR values were precise (<±0.55 mm), confirming proper mechanical and software alignment. CT number accuracy and nuclear medicine/CT registration tests confirmed precise anatomical-functional image overlay. Detector shielding and leakage tests showed minimal interference, supporting reliable imaging. Conclusion The SPECT/CT systems at NORI Hospital Islamabad met established NEMA standards for image quality. Acceptance testing validated detector performance and highlighted minor areas for improvement, such as periodic sensitivity calibration. Implementation of a structured quality control program ensures consistent equipment performance, optimal image quality, improved diagnostic accuracy, and superior patient care. Routine adherence to international standards is essential for maintaining high-quality nuclear medicine imaging practices.

title: Prognostic impact of risk organ involvement and metabolic parameters assessed by staging 18F-FDG PET/CT in pediatric Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
abstract: Objective To investigate the prognostic impact of risk organ involvement and baseline metabolic activity assessed by staging 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/computed tomography (CT) in newly diagnosed pediatric Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). Methods Thirty-two children with histologically confirmed LCH who underwent baseline 18F-FDG PET/CT were retrospectively analyzed. Age, disease extent (single-system vs. multisystem), risk organ involvement (RO- vs. RO+), and baseline metabolic parameters [maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax), SUVmean, metabolic tumor volume, total lesion glycolysis (TLG), and tumor-to-background ratio (TBR)] were evaluated for their association with progression or relapse. Optimal cut-offs were derived from receiver operating characteristic analysis (Youden index). Survival outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression models. Results Over a median follow-up of 33 months, disease progression or relapse occurred in 13 patients (40.6%) and was significantly associated with younger age (P = 0.040), higher SUVmax (P = 0.016), higher TBR (P = 0.007), and TLG (P = 0.033), multisystem LCH (P = 0.004), and risk organ positivity (P < 0.001). Risk-organ involvement was the strongest univariate predictor of adverse outcome (hazard ratio: 14.9, 95% confidence interval: 3.3-67; P < 0.001). Conclusion Baseline 18F-FDG PET/CT provides important prognostic information in pediatric LCH, with risk organ involvement emerging as the strongest univariate prognostic factor in this cohort, supporting its role in early risk stratification, suggesting a potential role in future risk-adapted treatment planning. Higher SUVmax, TBR, and TLG were associated with progression/relapse in group comparisons, whereas only SUVmax and TBR were significantly associated with progression-free survival in univariate Cox analysis.

title: Fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT-derived Metabolic Peritoneal Cancer Index for survival assessment in peritoneal carcinomatosis.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the association between the Metabolically active Peritoneal Cancer Index (M-PCI) derived from 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) and to assess its ability to predict overall survival (OS) in patients with peritoneal carcinomatosis. Methods This retrospective study included 107 patients with pathologically confirmed peritoneal carcinomatosis who underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT between October 2022 and July 2025. M-PCI was calculated using a PET-adapted Peritoneal Cancer Index approach based on metabolically active peritoneal lesions across 13 anatomical regions. Patients were stratified using an M-PCI cutoff value of 20, with the appropriateness of this threshold additionally explored using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Survival analysis was performed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and univariable and multivariable Cox regression models. Results During a median follow-up of 22 months, 78 deaths (72.9%) occurred. The median OS was 9 months. M-PCI was significantly associated with OS [hazard ratio = 1.050 per unit increase; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.019-1.082; P = 0.001]. Patients with M-PCI > 20 had significantly worse survival compared with those with M-PCI ≤ 20 (median OS = 3 vs. 10 months; log-rank P = 0.010), with nearly a two-fold increase in mortality risk (hazard ratio = 1.94; 95% CI = 1.14-3.32; P = 0.015). The prognostic impact of M-PCI was particularly pronounced in the gynecologic subgroup. In multivariable Cox regression analysis, M-PCI remained independently associated with OS after adjustment for tumor origin, treatment, extent of disease, ascites, and timing of peritoneal carcinomatosis (adjusted hazard ratio = 1.040; 95% CI = 1.002-1.080; P = 0.042). Conclusion M-PCI derived from 18F-FDG PET/CT is a significant predictor of OS in patients with peritoneal carcinomatosis. By integrating metabolic activity with spatial disease distribution, M-PCI may provide clinically relevant prognostic information and improve risk stratification in this patient population.

title: 18F-FDG PET/CT radiomics for prediction of BRCA mutations in high-grade serous ovarian cancer.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to develop and validate a 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography (CT)-based radiomics model for predicting BRCA mutation status in patients with advanced high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC). Methods A retrospective study of 124 patients with HGSOC who underwent preoperative PET/CT scans and BRCA mutation testing was conducted. The cohort was divided into training and internal validation sets using a 7 : 3 ratio. An external validation set of 25 patients was used to confirm model generalizability. Radiomic features were extracted from PET and CT images and used to build predictive models using logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, and decision tree classifiers. The models were evaluated for their predictive performance using metrics such as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, precision, sensitivity, and F1 score. A combined model incorporating radiomics, PET/CT metabolic parameters, and clinical variables was also constructed. In addition, the radiomics models were used to predict progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival in the training and internal validation cohorts. Results The logistic regression model showed the best performance, with AUCs of 94.79, 87.37, and 85.06% in the training, internal, and external validation cohorts, respectively. The combined model achieved the highest AUCs of 0.968, 0.932, and 0.960 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. Significant differences in PFS between risk groups were observed, while overall survival differences were not statistically significant. Conclusion The PET/CT-based radiomics model accurately predicts BRCA mutation status in HGSOC, potentially aiding in personalized treatment strategies.

title: Small-bowel incarceration and perforation through a hernia defect associated with a pubic fracture: a case report.
abstract: Background We encountered an extremely rare case of delayed small-bowel incarceration and perforation resulting from herniation through a defect at the site of a pubic fracture. Presentation of case A 69-year-old man receiving conservative treatment for a pubic fracture presented with abdominal pain approximately 3 months after the initial injury. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed free intraperitoneal air, ascites, and small-bowel dilatation, prompting emergency surgery. Intraoperative findings demonstrated ileal incarceration within a depression at the pubic fracture site, consistent with a Richter-type hernia accompanied by small-bowel perforation. Partial ileal resection with functional end-to-end anastomosis was performed, and the hernial defect was packed with omental tissue. Osteomyelitis observed at the fracture site was treated with antibiotics. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 40. Discussion Although rare, small-bowel herniation through a pelvic fracture site can result in incarceration and perforation. In this case, hernia repair was challenging because of contamination at the hernia site, which made mesh placement difficult, and the presence of a rigid hernia defect formed by an acquired bony defect, which was difficult to close with sutures. Based on a review of 11 cases reported between 2008 and 2026, including the present case, no standardized repair method has been established to date. Conclusion Treatment strategies should be individualized and include omental filling, fracture stabilization, and closure or management of the hernia.

title: Mesenteric vascular variations and Henle's trunk anatomy in right colon cancer surgery: implications for complete mesocolic excision and D2 lymphadenectomy.
abstract: Background Complete mesocolic excision (CME) with central lymphadenectomy represents the oncologic standard for right colon cancer surgery. However, vascular anatomical variability particularly involving the superior mesenteric vessels and Henle's gastrocolic trunk may substantially increase operative complexity and hemorrhagic risk. This study aimed to evaluate mesenteric vascular variations systematically and to analyze their implications for the quality and safety of CME/D2 right hemicolectomy. Materials and methods A retrospective descriptive single-center study was conducted at a tertiary referral university hospital. A total of 250 consecutive patients who underwent oncologic right hemicolectomy for histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma of the right colon between January 2020 and January 2025 were included. Clinical, radiological, operative, pathological, and postoperative data were analyzed. Mesenteric vascular anatomy was evaluated using CT angiography (available in 51.2% of cases) and correlated with intraoperative observations. The study was reported according to the STROBE criteria. Results The mean patient age was 64.5 ± 11.2 years (range 28-89) with slight female predominance (55.2%). Complicated presentations (obstruction, perforation, hemorrhage) occurred in 31.2% of cases. CT angiography was available for 128/250 patients (51.2%); its incomplete use was primarily attributable to emergency/complicated presentations (41.0% of the 122 non-angiography cases), resource/protocol constraints (34.4%), and adequate standard CT for planning (24.6%). The ileocolic and middle colic arteries were invariably present. The right colic artery was absent in 35.2% of patients, with variable origins when present. Henle's trunk was identified in 59.2% of patients, with three distinct venous configurations characterized. Open surgery was performed in 67.2% of cases. No major intraoperative vascular injury was recorded. Adequate lymph node harvest (≥12 nodes) was achieved in all patients (mean 24.6 ± 6.8 nodes). Anastomotic leakage occurred in 2.4% and 30-day mortality in 0.8%. Conclusion Mesenteric vascular variations are the rule rather than the exception during right colon cancer surgery. Preoperative CT angiography with vascular reconstruction appears to facilitate operative planning and anatomical orientation during CME/D2 lymphadenectomy. Standardized vascular-oriented dissection may improve oncologic quality while minimizing vascular complications.

title: Gastric duplication cyst mimicking an adrenal-region cyst: a diagnostic challenge.
abstract: Introduction and importance Gastric duplication cysts (GDCs) are rare congenital malformations that may mimic adrenal or retroperitoneal cysts. Misdiagnosis can delay proper management. We report a unique case of a GDC that was misdiagnosed as a left adrenal cyst, with reversible hyperreninemia and indirect hyperbilirubinemia. Presentation of case A 28-year-old asymptomatic man was incidentally found to have a left adrenal cyst on ultrasound. CT revealed a 4.1 × 5.5 cm non-enhancing unilocular cyst with preserved adrenal structure. Laboratory tests showed elevated upright plasma renin concentration (63.3 pg/mL) and indirect bilirubin (57.6 μmol/L). During laparoscopic excision, a cyst arising from the gastric fundus was identified. Pathology confirmed a non-communicating GDC lined by gastric mucosa and smooth muscle. Three months postoperatively, renin and bilirubin levels normalized. Clinical discussion Ectopic GDCs in the adrenal region are extremely rare and often misinterpreted radiologically. The postoperative normalization of renin and bilirubin raises a possible association, but the mechanisms remain speculative, and causality cannot be established from this single case. Intraoperative cyst-fluid analysis and multidisciplinary evaluation assist in accurate diagnosis. Complete resection provided definitive diagnosis and a favorable short-term outcome in the present case; however, longer follow-up is required to assess recurrence and sustained biochemical remission. Conclusion GDC should be considered in adrenal-region cystic lesions with atypical features. Total excision provides both definitive diagnosis and a favorable short-term outcome, although longer surveillance is required.

title: Simple hepatic cyst is not always simple - a case report of cystobiliary communication requiring hepatic resection.
abstract: Background Simple hepatic cysts are common and usually asymptomatic, but rarely may communicate with the intrahepatic biliary tree; unroofing alone can then result in postoperative bile leakage if this communication is not recognized. Case presentation We report a 74-year-old woman with multiple hepatic cysts, the largest measuring 11 cm and causing extrinsic gastric compression. Preoperative computed tomography (CT) suggested a simple cyst without evidence of biliary communication, and laparoscopic unroofing was planned. Needle decompression, however, yielded bile-like fluid indicating unsuspected cystobiliary communication; the procedure was therefore converted to laparoscopic left lateral sectionectomy. Her postoperative course was uneventful, without bile leakage. Conclusion In conclusion, a preoperatively "simple" hepatic cyst may harbor unsuspected cystobiliary communication that CT alone can miss. Intraoperative vigilance and willingness to convert to formal resection are essential when this complication is encountered.

title: Hydrocele stone presentation and crystallographic analysis: a unique case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance Hydroceles are typically benign fluid collections around the testes. Rarely, scrotal calculi, or "hydrocele stones," form within the tunica vaginalis, possibly due to chronic inflammation, torsion of the appendix testis, minor trauma, or other mechanisms. These stones are infrequently reported, and cases with detailed crystallographic analysis are exceptionally rare. Case presentation We present a 43-year-old male with bilateral hydroceles, a history of psoriasis and dyslipidemia, and prior right inguinal hernia repair. Ultrasound revealed a moderate right hydrocele and a small left hydrocele containing a 3 mm echogenic hydrocele stone, later found to measure 5 mm on direct intraoperative measurement. The patient underwent bilateral hydrocelectomy, during which the left hydrocele stone was retrieved. Crystallographic analysis revealed that the stone was composed of 80% calcium carbonate phosphate and 20% calcium carbonate. Postoperative recovery was uneventful. Clinical discussion Scrotal calculi are generally asymptomatic and often discovered incidentally during imaging or surgery. Their formation may involve inflammation, torsion, trauma, or parasitic infections. Crystallographic analysis provides valuable insights into stone composition, helping to distinguish these rare lesions from other scrotal pathologies. Conclusion Although hydrocele stones are rare and usually benign, further studies are needed to elucidate their pathogenesis, composition, and prevalence. Reporting such cases contributes to the understanding of this uncommon entity and aids in clinical recognition.

Scrotal calculi are generally asymptomatic and often discovered incidentally during imaging or surgery. Their formation may involve inflammation, torsion, trauma, or parasitic infections. Crystallographic analysis provides valuable insights into stone composition, helping to distinguish these rare lesions from other scrotal pathologies.

Conclusion

Although hydrocele stones are rare and usually benign, further studies are needed to elucidate their pathogenesis, composition, and prevalence. Reporting such cases contributes to the understanding of this uncommon entity and aids in clinical recognition.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) Syndrome Mimicking Bilateral Optic Neuritis.
abstract: Introduction Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is an idiopathic immune-related disorder that affects multiple organ systems, particularly targeting melanocytes in the uvea, ear, and meninges. It can sometimes present as subacute vision loss and or headache without other systemic features mimicking optic neuritis or Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, leading to an initial misdiagnosis. Case report A 36-year-old male presented with an acute onset and progressive diminution of vision in both eyes for 5 days. Fundus examination revealed papillitis. Brain MRI and CSF examination were normal. Serum NMO and MOG were negative. Considering bilateral optic neuritis, he was started on intravenous methylprednisolone therapy, following which his vision showed initial improvement, followed by deterioration after 3 days. The MRI was reviewed again and showed a subtle FLAIR hyperintensity just lateral to the optic nerve entry in the posterior pole, suggestive of choroidal thickening. Optical coherence tomography showed bilateral large Neurosensory retinal detachment and intraretinal fluid. Fundus fluorescein angiography showed multifocal pinpoint hyperfluorescent spots due to leakage from the retinal pigment epithelium and dye pooling in the subretinal space, suggestive of VKH syndrome. Visual acuity improved after 3 cycles of plasma exchange to 6/6 in the right eye and 6/12 in the left eye. Conclusion VKH should be considered in the differential diagnosis of any patient presenting with a history and examination suggestive of bilateral seronegative optic neuritis, even in the absence of characteristic extraocular manifestations of the disease.

title: Diagnostic Value and Forensic Applicability of Tissue-Based Findings in Suspected Fatal Electrocution: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Fatal electrocution remains a difficult diagnosis in forensic pathology, particularly when external electrical marks are absent or poorly preserved. Histopathology is commonly used as supportive evidence, but the diagnostic value of individual findings is uncertain. We systematically reviewed studies reporting histopathologic and ancillary tissue-based findings in suspected fatal electrocution or electrical injury. Twenty-seven primary studies with extractable tissue-level data were included. Skin electrical marks were the most frequently investigated target. Routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) findings included intraepidermal or subepidermal separation, coagulative necrosis, epidermal nuclear elongation or streaming, vacuolization, dermal collagen homogenization, and vascular changes. Comparative studies indicated that combinations of these findings may help distinguish electrical marks from flame burns or abrasions, although no feature was pathognomonic. Scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy or analysis (SEM-EDS/EDX) provided the strongest ancillary support through detection of metallization, particularly when conventional histology or histochemical stains were inconclusive. Cardiac studies described myofiber break-up, contraction bands, cardiomyolysis, microhemorrhages, and conduction-related changes, but these findings were generally nonspecific. Overall, tissue findings should be interpreted using a multimodal, context-dependent approach. Skin histology and metallization analysis offer the greatest diagnostic support, whereas cardiac and other internal-organ findings are mainly supportive or mechanistic.

title: Bilateral Hoffa's Fat Pad Ganglion Cysts with Subcutaneous Extension: A Rare Case Report.
abstract: Ganglion cysts within Hoffa's fat pad are an uncommon cause of anterior knee pain, with bilateral involvement being very rare. We report a unique case of a 42-year-old female presenting with bilateral Hoffa's fat pad ganglion cysts, complicated by subcutaneous extension and deep infrapatellar bursitis on the left side. Ultrasound-guided aspiration with corticosteroid injection provided symptomatic relief. This case highlights a rare combination of findings which was not previously documented in the literature and this report underscores the importance of bilateral ultrasound scan in diagnosis and individualized approach for management of anterior knee pain.

title: Robotic approach for OHVIRA syndrome: case report of an early diagnosis in a prepubertal girl.
abstract: Introduction OHVIRA (obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal agenesis) syndrome, also known as Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich syndrome, is a rare congenital anomaly of the female urogenital tract characterized by uterus didelphys, an obstructed hemivagina, and ipsilateral renal agenesis. It is typically diagnosed at puberty due to cyclic pelvic pain or hematocolpos. Early recognition in childhood is uncommon but may prevent serious complications. Case presentation We describe a 1-year-old girl in whom OHVIRA syndrome was incidentally identified during imaging performed for unrelated findings. Ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated right renal agenesis, uterine duplication, and an obstructed hemivagina. Diagnostic endoscopy confirmed vaginal duplication with a right atretic hemivagina and absence of the right ureteral orifice, suggesting an ectopic ureteral insertion. The patient underwent robotic-assisted right nephroureterectomy, partial hysterectomy, and excision of the right hemivagina without complications. She was discharged on postoperative day 2 and remains asymptomatic after 1 year of follow-up. Clinical discussion Early identification of OHVIRA syndrome is essential to prevent complications such as infection, pelvic abscess, endometriosis, and infertility. Robotic surgery offers excellent visualization, precise dissection, and safe reconstruction, particularly in deep pelvic regions. Compared with conventional approaches, it provides reduced postoperative pain, shorter hospital stays, and faster recovery. Conclusion Robotic-assisted surgery represents a safe and minimally invasive approach for the management of OHVIRA syndrome, even in very young patients, ensuring complete anatomical correction with minimal morbidity and rapid recovery.

title: H-type anorectovaginal fistula with anterior ectopic anus in a 15-month-old girl: a case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance H-type anorectovaginal fistula is a rare anorectal malformation characterized by an abnormal communication between the rectum and vagina despite a normally formed or near-normal anus. Diagnosis may be delayed due to the absence of obvious external anatomical abnormalities, making clinical recognition essential, particularly in resource-limited settings. Case presentation We report a 15-month-old girl presenting with fecal vaginal discharge and chronic constipation since early infancy. Clinical examination revealed an anterior ectopic stenotic anus with vaginal fecal contamination, consistent with H-type anorectovaginal fistula. Diagnosis was established clinically due to clear findings and financial constraints limiting access to advanced imaging modalities. Abdominal radiography demonstrated a loaded rectosigmoid colon, while abdominal ultrasonography was normal. The patient underwent limited posterior sagittal anorectoplasty with fistula division and reconstruction. The postoperative course was uneventful, and bowel management was initiated early. At 2-year follow-up, the patient demonstrated age-appropriate continence based on clinical assessment and parental reporting consistent with expected developmental stage, with no recurrence or complications. Clinical discussion H-type anorectovaginal fistula is an uncommon variant of anorectal malformations and may present diagnostic challenges due to subtle external findings. Management remains controversial because of anatomical variability; however, posterior sagittal anorectoplasty provides direct access for precise anatomical correction. In selected patients, single-stage repair without diversion can achieve favorable outcomes when conditions are optimal. Conclusion Careful clinical evaluation remains the cornerstone of diagnosis in rare anorectal malformations. Individualized surgical management based on anatomy and reconstructive principles can achieve good functional outcomes even in resource-limited environments.

title: Unusual location of sinonasal ossifying fibroma of the posterior ethmoid sinus: a case report and literature review.
abstract: Introduction and importance Ossifying fibroma is a benign, well-demarcated fibro-osseous neoplasm that most commonly affects the mandible and maxilla. Involvement of the paranasal sinuses is rare, and ethmoid sinus localization is particularly uncommon. Because sinonasal ossifying fibroma may mimic other fibro-osseous and osseous lesions radiologically, histopathologic confirmation and complete excision are important for diagnosis and disease control. Case presentation A 43-year-old Saudi man with well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a 6-month history of progressive right-sided nasal obstruction and frontal headache. He reported no history of epistaxis, visual disturbance, or anosmia. Computed tomography demonstrated a well-defined 2.5 × 1.6 × 2.3 cm sclerotic lesion with ground-glass matrix occupying the right posterior ethmoid air cells and abutting the skull base. Histopathology confirmed ossifying fibroma. The patient underwent complete endoscopic transnasal resection with skull base repair using a free autologous cartilage graft. The clinical course is summarized in Table 1. Recovery was uneventful, and he was discharged on postoperative day two. Clinical discussion Ethmoidal ossifying fibroma is rare and may present with nonspecific sinonasal symptoms. Complete excision is recommended for symptomatic sinonasal disease because incomplete removal is associated with recurrence. In selected cases, an endoscopic approach can provide direct visualization, avoid external approach-related morbidity, and allow skull base reconstruction when required. However, 4-month follow-up is insufficient to make definitive statements about long-term recurrence. Conclusion Posterior ethmoid ossifying fibroma is an uncommon presentation of a benign fibro-osseous tumor. Accurate diagnosis requires clinical, radiologic, and histopathologic correlation. Complete endoscopic resection with appropriate skull base repair can achieve favorable short-term outcomes in selected cases, but prolonged surveillance is necessary.

title: A rare case of lesser omental hernia in a male patient following total colectomy.
abstract: Introduction and importance A lesser omental hernia is a rare internal hernia in which intestinal loops become entrapped through a defect in the lesser omentum, potentially causing bowel obstruction. Its diagnosis is challenging because of nonspecific symptoms that resemble those of other gastrointestinal diseases. This report presents a case of lesser omental hernia following total colectomy. Case presentation A 65-year-old male with a history of laparoscopic total colectomy for ulcerative colitis 4 years prior presented with acute abdominal pain and distension. Computed tomography (CT) revealed a closed-loop small-bowel obstruction, leading to emergency surgery. Intraoperatively, no adhesions were found, but nearly the entire small intestine had herniated through a small foramen in the lesser omentum, passing dorsally behind the stomach. The intestine was repositioned, and the foramen was sutured closed. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 15, with no recurrence observed at the 6-month follow-up examination. Clinical discussion A lesser omental hernia may occur after colectomy due to iatrogenic disruption of the gastrocolic ligament. This case represented a type II hernia, with the small intestine prolapsing from the retrogastric space through a defect in the lesser omentum. A review of eight post-colectomy cases showed that all were type II. Diagnosis is difficult, but CT findings such as anteriorly displaced, dilated bowel loops and gastric distortion are key. Careful CT evaluation and intraoperative identification are essential for appropriate diagnosis and treatment. Conclusion A lesser omental hernia can occur after total colectomy. CT imaging is valuable for diagnosis, and surgical intervention is often required.

title: Splenic hematoma following ERCP for obstructive jaundice requiring splenectomy: a case report and literature review.
abstract: Introduction and importance Splenic injury following endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is an exceptionally rare but potentially life-threatening complication. Case presentation We report the case of a female patient admitted with obstructive jaundice and suspected periampullary malignancy associated with markedly elevated CA 19-9 levels. Following ERCP, abdominal computed tomography demonstrated a large subcapsular splenic hematoma. The patient underwent splenectomy, cholecystectomy, hepaticojejunostomy, and Roux-en-Y reconstruction. Histopathological examination confirmed traumatic splenic injury without evidence of malignancy. The postoperative course was complicated by pancreatic fistula, which was successfully managed conservatively. Clinical discussion ERCP-related splenic injury remains a rare complication with nonspecific clinical manifestations that may delay diagnosis. A review of the literature demonstrates substantial variability in clinical presentation and management, ranging from conservative treatment to splenectomy. Conclusion This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of ERCP-related splenic hematoma in patients undergoing evaluation for suspected pancreatic head malignancy. Early recognition, prompt cross-sectional imaging, and individualized multidisciplinary management are essential for achieving favorable outcomes. In selected patients, modification of the operative strategy according to intraoperative findings may be lifesaving.

title: Superficial squamous cell carcinoma arising in Laimer's diverticulum: a rare case highlighting the importance of anatomical differentiation.
abstract: Introduction Laimer's diverticulum (LD) is a rare pharyngoesophageal diverticulum that originates from the posterior wall of the cervical esophagus and beneath the cricopharyngeal muscle (CPM). Carcinoma arising in pharyngoesophageal diverticula occurs predominantly in association with Zenker's diverticulum (ZD), whereas its occurrence in LD is exceptionally rare. We report a rare case of superficial squamous cell carcinoma that originated in LD. Case presentation A 78-year-old man with a known esophageal diverticulum presented with a 9-year history of progressive dysphagia and regurgitation of food. Esophagography and contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a large posterior diverticulum originating from the cervical esophagus below the cricoid cartilage. Diverticulectomy was performed through a left cervical approach. Intraoperative findings confirmed that the diverticulum originated from the posterior wall of the cervical esophagus, inferior to the CPM, consistent with LD. Histopathological examination revealed an intra-diverticular 15 mm × 10 mm squamous cell carcinoma in situ (pT1a-EP). Surgical margins were negative, and the postoperative course was uneventful. Discussion Accurate anatomical differentiation among types of cervical esophageal diverticula is essential because treatment strategies may differ substantially among LD, ZD, and Killian-Jamieson diverticulum. Endoscopic identification may be difficult because retained food debris, chronic inflammatory changes, and the narrow diverticular lumen can conceal superficial lesions; meticulous cleaning and enhanced endoscopic observation, including narrow-band imaging or Lugol chromoendoscopy, may improve detection in similar cases. Misdiagnosis of LD as ZD may result in inappropriate treatment selection, particularly when endoscopic septotomy is considered. Conclusion We report a rare case of superficial squamous cell carcinoma originating in LD. Careful anatomical assessment is essential for accurate diagnosis and appropriate surgical management of cervical esophageal diverticula. This case underscores the importance of early surgical excision or regular surveillance when cervical esophageal diverticula are managed nonoperatively.

title: Osteoid osteoma of the talus adjacent to the subtalar joint: a rare location and diagnostic challenge.
abstract: Introduction and importance Osteoid osteoma is a common benign bone tumor, but lesions located in the talus, especially those adjacent to the subtalar joint, are relatively rare and prone to misdiagnosis. Its clinical and imaging manifestations are often atypical, which can lead to delayed diagnosis and inappropriate conservative treatment. Accurate imaging evaluation and appropriate surgical management are critical for symptom relief and functional recovery. Case presentation We present a 20-year-old male with chronic left ankle pain that worsened at night and with weight-bearing. Initial MRI suggested bone marrow edema and ligament injury, leading to a misdiagnosis of ankle synovitis and sprain. Subsequent CT clearly identified a 5-mm nidus at the medial inferior margin of the left talus. The patient underwent open resection with intraoperative CT-guided K-wire localization. Postoperative histopathological examination confirmed osteoid osteoma. At the 1-year follow-up, the patient was pain-free and had fully resumed daily activities. Clinical discussion Talar osteoid osteoma is prone to misdiagnosis because its symptoms resemble those of ankle sprain, synovitis, or impingement. CT is the gold standard for detecting the nidus, while MRI frequently shows nonspecific bone marrow edema. Surgical excision remains a reliable treatment method. CT-guided K-wire localization improves accuracy, minimizes bone damage, and ensures complete resection, avoiding incomplete ablation and the recurrence risk associated with percutaneous radiofrequency ablation. Conclusion Osteoid osteoma of the talus is a rare but significant cause of chronic ankle pain and is easily misdiagnosed. CT is essential for early and accurate diagnosis. For juxta-articular lesions, CT-guided K-wire localization followed by open resection is safe and effective, completely relieving symptoms and achieving good long-term outcomes.

title: Endovascular salvage of graft hepatic artery dissection with intrahepatic extension following right lobe living donor liver transplantation: a case report with literature review.
abstract: Introduction Hepatic artery complications after liver transplantation are uncommon but potentially catastrophic because the biliary tree depends entirely on the arterial blood supply. Graft hepatic artery dissection (GHAD) is extremely rare following living donor liver transplantation (LDLT), and optimal management strategies remain unclear. Case presentation A 68-year-old man with hepatocellular carcinoma and underlying alcohol-related cirrhosis underwent right-lobe LDLT. During donor hepatectomy, intimal dissection of the graft hepatic artery, extending deep into the liver parenchyma, was identified. After arterial reconstruction, intraoperative Doppler ultrasound demonstrated absent arterial flow. The abdomen was closed, and the patient was transferred for urgent endovascular intervention. Angiography confirmed compromised arterial inflow, and a drug-eluting stent was deployed across the arterial anastomosis, followed by catheter-directed thrombolysis using alteplase. Postoperatively, the patient developed intra-abdominal bleeding requiring emergency re-laparotomy for hemostasis. Despite this complication, hepatic arterial perfusion was successfully restored. Liver function gradually improved, and follow-up imaging confirmed adequate graft perfusion. The patient was discharged 3 weeks after transplantation with preserved graft function. Discussion GHAD is a rare but serious vascular complication that may result in graft ischemia, biliary complications, and graft failure if not promptly treated. When surgical revision is not feasible, endovascular techniques - including stent placement and thrombolysis - can serve as effective salvage strategies. However, thrombolytic therapy carries a significant risk of hemorrhagic complications, requiring careful postoperative monitoring. Conclusion Early diagnosis and multidisciplinary management are essential for the successful salvage of GHAD after LDLT.

title: Physical Evaluation of Focal Spot Size and Phantom Thickness in Coronary CT Angiography Using Super-Resolution Deep Learning Reconstruction.
abstract: Objective To compare images with small and large focal spot sizes under clinical tube current limits across different subject thicknesses in the heart region using super-resolution deep learning reconstruction (SRDLR) to elucidate image quality behavior. Methods We conducted quantitative assessments to compare small and large focal spot size images. The quantitative assessment involved imaging phantoms with 5 different diameters under coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) conditions, followed by SRDLR reconstruction. We calculated the noise power spectrum (NPS) to evaluate the frequency response of image noise in uniform phantom material. Spatial resolution was analyzed by measuring the task-based transfer function (TTF) for sections simulating iodine within the phantom. Results In the NPS, for phantom diameters between 16 and 31 cm, small focal spot size images exhibited higher noise than large focal spot size images. However, for a 36 cm-diameter phantom, the small focal spot size image had less noise in the high-frequency region. TTF values were better for small focal spot size images, but the difference decreased with increasing phantom diameter, becoming negligible at 31 cm. Conclusions The study clarified how focal spot size affects image quality in CCTA under maximum dose constraints, suggesting that optimal image quality can be achieved by appropriately selecting the focal spot size according to subject thickness.

title: Super-Resolution Deep Learning Reconstruction for 3-Dimensional T1-Weighted Gradient-Echo Imaging in Contrast-Enhanced Liver MRI: Comparison With Conventional and Standard Deep Learning Reconstructions.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the image quality of super-resolution deep learning reconstruction (SR-DLR) for 3-dimensional (3D) T1-weighted gradient-echo (GRE) imaging in contrast-enhanced MRI, compared with conventional reconstruction (Conv.) and standard deep learning reconstruction (DLR). Materials and methods This retrospective study included 50 patients (mean age: 71.5 y) with 76 hepatic lesions who underwent contrast-enhanced dynamic liver MRI at 3T. Portal venous phase images were reconstructed using Conv., DLR, and SR-DLR. Quantitative analyses measured liver signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast ratio (CR) between liver parenchyma and lesions, edge rise distance (ERD), and edge rise slope (ERS). Qualitative assessments of image noise, sharpness, contrast, motion artifacts, overall image quality, and lesion conspicuity were performed independently by 2 radiologists using a 5-point scale. Coronal multiplanar reformatted (MPR) images were also evaluated. Statistical comparisons were performed using the Friedman test with Bonferroni correction. Results Liver SNR was comparable between SR-DLR and DLR. SR-DLR produced sharper edges (lower ERD, higher ERS) and higher lesion-to-liver CR than Conv. and DLR (P<0.001). The overall CR differences were primarily driven by cystic lesions, whereas improvements in malignant lesions were modest. Qualitatively, SR-DLR received the highest ratings for sharpness, overall image quality, and lesion conspicuity, particularly on MPR images (P<0.001). SR-DLR images exhibited slightly higher image noise and motion-related artifacts than DLR. Conclusion SR-DLR improved spatial resolution, sharpness, and lesion conspicuity in contrast-enhanced MRI compared with Conv. and DLR, indicating potential to improve the diagnostic performance of dynamic liver MRI.

title: Multiparametric Whole-Body MRI Protocols in Contemporary Clinical Practice: Indications, Technical Considerations, and Emerging Applications.
abstract: Multiparametric whole-body MRI (WB-MRI) is an advanced cross-sectional imaging technique that integrates anatomic sequences into functional modalities, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) mapping and Dixon-based imaging. WB-MRI can evaluate the body from the vertex to the feet in a single session, offering advantages such as generating important biomarkers, robust musculoskeletal tissue assessment, high signal-to-noise ratio, and speed optimization, among others. This review examines current evidence and provides recommendations for multiparametric WB-MRI across a broad spectrum of oncologic and nononcologic indications, including multiple myeloma, lymphoma, melanoma, metastatic prostate cancer, cancer predisposition syndromes, MSK tumors, inflammatory arthritis, and diffuse neuromuscular disorders. Readers will gain an understanding of key technical considerations, including field strength selection, coil configuration, sequence design, and protocol optimization, that radiologists must navigate when implementing WB-MRI in clinical practice. Emerging applications such as AI-assisted lesion segmentation, automated quantitative biomarker analysis, and accelerated image reconstruction are also discussed, which spotlight the evolving role of WB-MRI in disease characterization and the following treatment response. As protocols become more standardized and evidence continues to grow, this review equips radiologists with a practical framework for incorporating multiparametric WB-MRI into contemporary clinical and research settings.

title: Clinical Utility of Ovarian-Adnexal Reporting and Data System Magnetic Resonance Imaging for Risk Stratifying Adnexal Masses: An Assessment of Diagnostic Efficacy and Interrater Reliability.
abstract: Objective Accurate characterization of adnexal masses is essential for determining malignancy risk and guiding clinical management. While the O-RADS MRI system provides standardized risk stratification, the impact of MRI acquisition protocols on diagnostic performance and interrater reliability remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of O-RADS MRI, assess interrater reliability between readers with different experience levels, and investigate the contribution of dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI to reader concordance. Materials and methods A total of 387 patients with 496 adnexal masses were retrospectively analyzed. Histopathologic diagnosis was obtained through surgery or biopsy, while lesions without histopathology were considered benign if they remained stable or regressed during at least 9 months of imaging follow-up. Two radiologists with different levels of experience independently evaluated all MRI examinations using the O-RADS MRI lexicon. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis with area under the curve (AUC). Interobserver agreement was evaluated using the Cohen κ statistic. Results Both readers demonstrated high diagnostic performance. Sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 96.8%, 94.1%, and 95.2% for reader 1, and 96.8%, 92.9%, and 94.4% for reader 2. AUC values were 0.976 (95% CI: 0.940-0.992) and 0.970 (95% CI: 0.933-0.989), respectively. Interobserver agreement was substantial for benign-malignant classification (κ = 0.757; 95% CI: 0.624-0.889) and excellent for O-RADS category assignment (κ = 0.941; 95% CI: 0.919-0.962). Diagnostic performance was comparable between dynamic and nondynamic protocols; however, dynamic MRI demonstrated higher interobserver agreement, particularly for lesion classification. Conclusion O-RADS MRI provides high diagnostic performance and strong interobserver agreement in the evaluation of adnexal masses. Although dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI does not significantly improve diagnostic accuracy, it may enhance reader concordance, particularly in lesions with equivocal imaging features.

title: Whole-Body MRI in Neurocutaneous Syndromes: Imaging Phenotypes, Surveillance Strategies, and Pitfalls.
abstract: Neurocutaneous syndromes associated with peripheral nerve sheath tumors (PNSTs), particularly neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and schwannomatosis (SWN), are characterized by variable tumor burden and multisystem involvement. Whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (WB-MRI) has emerged as an important imaging technique for screening, surveillance, lesion characterization, and treatment monitoring in both pediatric and adult populations. Updated molecular and imaging-based classification systems have further refined characterization of PNST phenotypes. In NF1, WB-MRI enables detection of internal tumor burden, longitudinal assessment of plexiform neurofibromas (PNs), and risk stratification for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) development. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) mapping improves differentiation between benign and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors with emerging data on premalignant precursor lesions called atypical neurofibromatous neoplasms of uncertain biologic potential (ANNUBP). In SWN, evolving diagnostic criteria and genotype-phenotype correlations have increased the importance of imaging in young patients presenting with solitary schwannoma or meningioma. WB-MRI can establish internal tumor burden, define disease extent, and support surveillance strategies across genetically defined SWN subtypes. This review summarizes current applications of WB-MRI in NF1 and SWN, including imaging phenotypes, surveillance strategies, advanced imaging biomarkers, treatment response assessment, and common technical and interpretive pitfalls.

title: Accelerated Body Composition Analysis in Whole-body MRI Using CycleGAN-based T2-HASTE Synthesis From Fast Whole-body Localizers.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate whether CycleGAN-based synthesis of T2-HASTE images from routinely acquired fast whole-body localizer (FWBL) can support accelerated body composition analysis (BCA) by preserving sufficient information for an established T2-HASTE-based BCA pipeline to generate measurements comparable to those derived from reference T2-HASTE images. Materials and methods This retrospective single-center proof-of-concept study included 468 patients (53% female, mean age 51±18 y) who underwent WB-MRI with FWBL and T2-HASTE between March 2012 and December 2025, 431 (92%) of whom were examined from 2023 onward. A CycleGAN model was trained to generate synthetic T2-HASTE images from registered FWBL and T2-HASTE images. Fully automated MRI-based BCA was conducted on synthetic and reference T2-HASTE images using a fixed pretrained BCA model, focusing on 5 key segmentation compartments: subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT), muscle, abdominal cavity, thoracic cavity, and bone, with subsequent region-specific volumetric analyses of SAT, muscle, and bone in the thoracic, abdominal, and whole-body regions. Derived BCA markers included the Sarcopenia Index (muscle-to-bone ratio) and the muscle-to-SAT ratio. Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman analysis, including mean bias expressed in absolute units and as a percentage of the mean reference volume, median absolute percentage error, Pearson correlation, and weighted Cohen kappa for tertile-based stratification. Segmentation overlap was evaluated using Sørensen-Dice similarity coefficients. In addition, a qualitative reader evaluation was performed by 4 radiologists across 30 cases. Results Mean percentage bias across the thoracic, abdominal, and whole-body regions was -0.05%, 3.51%, and 2.91% for muscle, -0.19%, -1.21%, and 0.71% for SAT, and -7.10%, -8.86%, and -6.30% for bone, respectively. Median absolute percentage error remained low for muscle (2.96% to 3.52%) and SAT (2.03% to 3.71%), whereas bone showed the highest relative error (5.93% to 8.26%). Tertile-based stratification agreement was high, particularly for the muscle-to-SAT ratio, with unchanged tertile assignment in 89.4% of thoracic, 93.6% of abdominal, and 95.7% of whole-body analyses (κ=0.92, 0.95, and 0.97, respectively). For the Sarcopenia Index, unchanged tertile assignment was 68.1%, 80.9%, and 87.2%, respectively (κ=0.76, 0.86, and 0.90). Segmentation overlap was high across the main compartments, with mean Sørensen-Dice coefficients of 0.90 for SAT, 0.87 for muscle, 0.94 for the abdominal cavity, and 0.91 for the thoracic cavity, whereas bone showed lower overlap (0.76). Qualitative evaluation showed positive ratings for both synthetic image utility and segmentation plausibility, with the synthetic T2 representation rated as providing added value over FWBL for coarse body composition assessment on a 5-point Likert scale, where 1 indicated strong disagreement, and 5 indicated strong agreement (mean: 4.52, median: 5). Conclusions Combining FWBL MRI with CycleGAN-based image synthesis yielded BCA measurements that closely matched those from reference T2-HASTE images and largely preserved body composition stratification. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of deriving quantitative BCA information from routinely acquired WB-MRI localizer data and support further investigation of accelerated MRI-based BCA approaches using simplified acquisitions.

title: The Challenge of Rendering Abnormalities Accurately Using Deep Learning-Based Reconstruction in Accelerated Brain MRI: A Disproportionate Loss of Clinically Relevant Image Information at Higher Rates of Acceleration.
abstract: Objectives Deep learning (DL)-based reconstruction methods can substantially accelerate MRI acquisition while preserving image quality relative to traditional techniques. However, concerns remain regarding their ability to accurately reconstruct abnormalities at higher acceleration factors. This study quantitatively assesses the impact of higher-order acceleration on image quality in DL-reconstructed brain MRI in normal and abnormal cases, emphasizing the utmost need to render abnormal findings accurately. Materials and methods Raw k-space image data from 5847 brain MRI examinations (fastMRI) were used. A radiologist-annotated subset of 1001 examinations (fastMRI+) served as the test set; the remainder were split into training (n=3715) and validation (n=1131) sets. Images were retrospectively undersampled (acceleration factors 2 to 12) and reconstructed using an end-to-end variational network. Image quality metrics, including normalized mean squared error (NMSE), structural similarity index measure (SSIM), and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), were computed within bounding-box annotations containing abnormalities and in size-matched normal control regions, and at the slice-level. The region-by-acceleration interaction was tested using linear mixed-effects models with a subject-level random intercept. Results All metrics demonstrated progressive degradation with increasing acceleration across slice-level and bounding-box-level analyses. At lower acceleration rates, bounding boxes with and without abnormalities showed comparable image quality. However, above 4-fold acceleration, NMSE within abnormal regions exhibited a notably sharper increase with rising acceleration compared to normal regions, while abnormal regions demonstrated a significantly faster decline in PSNR and SSIM. This nonsymmetric information loss was particularly evident for NMSE at higher acceleration rates. The region-by-acceleration interaction was statistically significant for all 3 metrics at both levels (all adjusted P<0.001), with the effect largest and most consistent for NMSE. Conclusions Our findings demonstrate a disproportionate, pathology-localized degradation of reconstruction quality as acceleration increases. This emphasizes the importance of rigorous clinical assessment of image quality in DL-MRI reconstruction, particularly at higher undersampling rates, highlighting the need for reconstruction strategies tailored to maintaining diagnostically critical features.

title: 18F-FDG PET/CT Manifestations of a Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor Presenting With Predominant Hepatic and Peritoneal Metastases.
abstract: A 70-year-old man presented with abdominal pain. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated multiple large space-occupying lesions in the liver. An 18F-FDG PET/CT scan was subsequently performed to identify the primary tumor, revealing extensive hepatic and peritoneal metastases. Histopathologic examination ultimately confirmed the diagnosis of a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). GIST typically presents as a primary solid mass arising from the stomach or other parts of the gastrointestinal tract. In this case, however, the predominant imaging findings were multiple hepatic metastases and extensive peritoneal dissemination, with the primary tumor being less conspicuous.

title: 177Lu-FAPI-2286 Radioligand Therapy in Refractory Scalp Melanoma.
abstract: A 66-year-old man with inoperable malignant scalp melanoma, refractory to immunotherapy, underwent 99mTc-HYNIC-TOC SPECT/CT for evaluating the possibility of radioligand therapy with 177Lu-DOTATATE, which demonstrated no tracer uptake in scalp lesions, precluding 177Lu-DOTATATE therapy. Subsequent disease progression prompted 99mTc-FAPI-46 SPECT/CT, which showed intense tracer uptake in lesions and prompted radioligand therapy with 177Lu-FAPI-2286. After 4 cycles of treatment, all lesions showed regression and he was referred for tumor resection. This case illustrates the clinical utility of FAPI-based theranostic and shows 99mTc-FAPI SPECT/CT can directly inform targeted radioligand therapy using 177Lu-FAPI, thereby expanding therapeutic options in melanoma management.

title: [18F]FDG PET/CT Findings of Primary Uterine Dysgerminoma: A Case Report.
abstract: Primary uterine dysgerminoma is a rare malignant neoplasm. We reported the [18F]FDG PET/CT findings in a case of primary uterine dysgerminoma in a 60-year-old woman with dull lower abdominal pain. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a posterior uterine mass suspicious for sarcoma. [18F]FDG PET/CT demonstrated uterine morphologic distortion, marked volumetric enlargement, and diffusely increased FDG uptake, suggestive of uterine malignancy. MRI revealed a posterior uterine wall mass, exhibiting hypoenhancement relative to the normal myometrium with internal enhancing septa, suggestive of uterine leiomyosarcoma. The woman underwent total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. The uterine mass was diagnosed as dysgerminoma on histopathology and immunohistochemistry.

title: Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Evaluation of Papillary Renal Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) comprises approximately 90% of malignancy in the kidney. Early stage RCC is often asymptomatic. The majority of RCC are incidentally found on imaging ordered for unrelated medical indications. When diagnosed at an early stage, the survival or even cure rate is high. With more progressive stages, the outcome is less favorable. Tumor-induced angiogenesis affects blood flow in tumors such that patterns of perfusion can be utilized for diagnosis. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) takes advantage of the vascular architecture and provides a real-time assessment of vascularity, helping differentiate between solid and cystic masses. CEUS is a favorable tool for evaluation of indeterminate renal lesions due to its specificity for solid enhancing components, safety profile, and relatively low cost when compared with other imaging modalities including computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This case highlights the sensitivity of contrast-enhanced ultrasound for detecting blood flow in a patient with papillary RCC.

title: A Novel Ultrasonographic Approach to Baastrup Disease (Kissing Spines Syndrome).
abstract: Baastrup disease (BD) is characterized by the close approximation of adjacent spinous processes, interspinous bursitis, and degenerative changes. Although BD is a well-known cause of chronic low back pain, it is often misdiagnosed due to limited clinical awareness and reliance on conventional imaging. While radiography, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging remain central to the diagnosis of BD, ultrasound (US) can also identify interspinous bursitis, reduced interspinous space, and ligament involvement. Herein, we present two cases of BD with corresponding US images. This report aims to emphasize the diagnostic utility of US in detecting characteristic features of BD and to explore its potential role in therapeutic guidance. In this context, broader integration of US into clinical practice may improve the recognition and management of this frequently overlooked cause of low back pain.

title: Secondary CT Signs of Occult Craniofacial Fractures in Patients With Head and Facial Trauma.
abstract: Objective To characterize secondary CT signs, anatomic distribution, diagnostic delay, and clinical consequences among patients with head and facial trauma who had subsequently confirmed occult craniofacial fractures on CT imaging. Methods A retrospective data set was generated for 80 eligible cases, covering December 2022 through December 2025. Eligible CT examinations were initial head, facial, or maxillofacial trauma CT scans in which no definite fracture was reported initially or the fracture was visible only through subtle secondary signs, followed by confirmation on subspecialty re-review, thin-section multiplanar reconstruction, cone-beam CT, follow-up CT, or intraoperative correlation. Variables included demographic factors, trauma mechanism, fracture site, secondary CT sign, acquisition and reconstruction features, artifacts, confirmation method, time to detection, and whether diagnosis changed management. Proportions were summarized with Wilson 95% CIs. Skewed time intervals were summarized as medians with IQRs. Associations with clinically significant management change were explored with univariate odds ratios and a parsimonious logistic model. Results The most common sites were the mandibular condyle (17/80) and the nasal bone (16/80). Management changed in 30/80 cases (37.5%; 95% CI: 27.7-48.5). Median time to detection was 24 hours (IQR=10-37). Univariate analysis showed higher odds of management change with axial-only reconstruction, moderate motion artifact, and delayed detection of 24 hours or longer; the multivariable model showed directionally similar but imprecise estimates. Conclusion Occult craniofacial fractures on CT clustered in thin cortical and complex multiplanar regions. Secondary signs such as sinus fluid, orbital emphysema, fat stranding, periodontal air, and joint-space asymmetry were central to recognition. Systematic thin-section multiplanar review may reduce delayed diagnosis and improve clinically relevant triage.

Proportions were summarized with Wilson 95% CIs. Skewed time intervals were summarized as medians with IQRs. Associations with clinically significant management change were explored with univariate odds ratios and a parsimonious logistic model.

Results

The most common sites were the mandibular condyle (17/80) and the nasal bone (16/80). Management changed in 30/80 cases (37.5%; 95% CI: 27.7-48.5). Median time to detection was 24 hours (IQR=10-37). Univariate analysis showed higher odds of management change with axial-only reconstruction, moderate motion artifact, and delayed detection of 24 hours or longer; the multivariable model showed directionally similar but imprecise estimates.

Conclusion

Occult craniofacial fractures on CT clustered in thin cortical and complex multiplanar regions. Secondary signs such as sinus fluid, orbital emphysema, fat stranding, periodontal air, and joint-space asymmetry were central to recognition. Systematic thin-section multiplanar review may reduce delayed diagnosis and improve clinically relevant triage.

title: Clinical Diagnostic Challenges in Childhood Pilomatrixoma: A Retrospective Study of 74 Patients.
abstract: Pilomatrixoma is a common, but frequently misdiagnosed, benign skin tumor in childhood. This retrospective study evaluated the clinical diagnostic challenges, anatomic distribution, and surgical outcomes of pediatric pilomatrixoma in 74 patients aged 0 to 18 years with a histopathologically confirmed diagnosis, treated between 2017 and 2026. The mean age was 10.4 years, with a female-to-male ratio of 1.5:1. Lesions were located in the head and neck in 67.6% of the patients, most often in the neck (42.0%), with the posterior neck being the single most common subsite, with a median greatest diameter of 1.0 cm, and 24.3% of the patients had multiple lesions. The preliminary clinical diagnosis matched the histopathologic diagnosis in only 4.1% of cases, and the radiologic diagnosis matched the histopathologic diagnosis in only 1.4%. Preoperative imaging reliably detected a mass but rarely characterized it specifically as pilomatrixoma, and 35.1% of patients did not undergo preoperative imaging. Complete surgical excision was performed in all patients according to aesthetic principles. Postoperative complications occurred in 5.4% and true local recurrence in 1.4% of patients; 3 additional patients developed metachronous lesions at distinct anatomic sites during follow-up, and no patient had an associated syndrome or malignant transformation. Pediatric pilomatrixoma shows strikingly low preoperative diagnostic accuracy, underscoring the need for a high index of suspicion with histopathology as the diagnostic gold standard. Complete excision according to aesthetic principles yields a low recurrence rate and excellent cosmetic outcome, and metachronous lesions warrant long-term follow-up.

title: The Anatomy of Sentinel Vein Based on Cadaver and Ultrasound.
abstract: Background The sentinel vein (SV) plays a vital role in temporal rhytidectomy and temporal cosmetic injection procedures. Accurate anatomic localization and morphologic data of this vein are currently lacking. This study delineates its detailed anatomic characteristics through cadaver anatomy and ultrasonic examination. Methods Twenty cadavers (40 temporal regions) were dissected, and 20 healthy volunteers (40 temporal regions) underwent ultrasonographic examination. The course, caliber, spatial depth, tributaries, and superficial projection of the SV were documented, along with its positional relationship to the frontal branch of the facial nerve. Results The SV presents a mean of 2.4 tributaries and can be categorized into 6 confluence types based on tributary course. The vein comprises a horizontal segment and a vertical segment. The horizontal segment travels superficially parallel to the skin within the plane between the superficial temporal fascia and subcutaneous fat before transitioning into the vertical segment, which ultimately drains into the middle temporal vein (MTV). The superficial projection of the SV and its anatomic relationship with the frontal branch of the facial nerve exhibit relatively consistent anatomic features. Conclusions This study established 6 anatomic classification patterns of the SV and quantified its superficial projection landmarks. These findings provide critical anatomic references for temporal rhytidectomy and temporal cosmetic filler injection.

title: Postoperative PLR Slope for Early Warning of Colorectal Anastomotic Leakage.
abstract: Background Anastomotic leakage (AL) after colorectal resection is often confirmed between postoperative days (PODs) 4 and 8. We evaluated whether the POD1-to-3 platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) "rising slope" in routine blood counts provides an earlier warning of ISREC grade B/C AL. Methods In a prospective single-center cohort (2021 to 2025), analyses used a POD3 landmark among patients who were alive and without an AL diagnosis through POD3. PLR slope was derived from POD1 to 3 blood draw timestamps and modeled at 10 PLR units/day. Thirty-day International Study Group of Rectal Cancer (ISREC) grade B/C AL was adjudicated blinded using CT with IV contrast (± rectal contrast when feasible) and/or endoscopy/operative findings. First logistic regression with bootstrap optimism correction estimated the association and AUC. A sensitivity-first operating threshold, selected using nested resampling and CRP/NLR comparators, was evaluated. Results A total of 101 participants developed 30-day AL after the POD3 landmark assessment. PLR slope was associated with AL (OR=1.31 per 10 units/day; 95% CI: 1.02-1.89; P=0.039) with AUC 0.74 (95% CI: 0.58-0.86) and optimism-corrected AUC 0.72. The sensitivity-first threshold achieved sensitivity 83.0%, specificity 61.0%, PPV 12.0%, and NPV 98.3%, with a median lead-time of 2 days (IQR=1 to 3) from POD3 assessment to radiologic confirmation. In the CRP subset, AUCs were 0.67 for CRP POD3, 0.70 for CRP slope, and 0.62 for NLR POD3 (all P>0.20 vs. PLR slope). Decision-curve analysis favored PLR-slope triage over imaging-all-or-none triage across 5% to 12% threshold probabilities. Conclusions In our study, the POD1-to-3 PLR slope is a low-cost, POD3-available rule-out adjunct that may provide earlier warning before radiologic confirmation of clinically relevant AL. Multicenter validation is required to confirm generalizability, finalize operating thresholds, and quantify downstream imaging and outcome trade-offs.
